summary: This document describes how a node can report its locally known Segment Routing (SR) Policy information using BGP Link State (BGP-LS). External components can use it for path computation, reoptimization, service placement, and network visualization.

eli5.summary: Routers keep private notes about the special routes they use. This gives them a standard way to share the notes with a central planner who can see the whole map.

questions: advertise segment routing policy using bgp
what is the sr policy candidate path nlri
how do controllers learn sr policies
subtitle: How a router reports the state of its Segment Routing policies to controllers and path computation tools using BGP-LS.

tldr.problem: Controllers, path computation elements and management systems need to know the configuration and state of every SR Policy in the network, but headend routers may not speak PCEP to report it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a new BGP-LS NLRI type, the SR Policy Candidate Path NLRI (type 5), plus a set of TLVs that report a candidate path's state, binding SID, constraints, and segment lists.
tldr.outcome: External components can collect SR Policy information over the same BGP-LS protocol they already use for topology, either from the headend or from a PCE reporting on its behalf.

today: RFC 9857 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025, and the unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on BGP-LS in RFC 9552 and the SR Policy architecture in RFC 9256.

sections.title: Why Report SR Policy State
sections.content:
An SR Policy, as defined in RFC 9256, has one or more candidate paths. At a given time only one may be active, meaning installed in forwarding and usable for steering traffic. Each candidate path can have one or more SID lists, and when several are active, traffic is load balanced over them. This document reports state at the level of the individual candidate path.

Controllers that know both the topology and the SR Policy state can optimize the network. The RFC gives several cases: a stateful PCE (RFC 8231) doing path optimization, a management-based PCE architecture (RFC 4655) where headends may not implement PCEP, parent and child PCEs in multi-area or multi-AS networks, a centralized controller deciding service placement, and a network management system offering visualization.

Since BGP already distributes link-state and traffic engineering information to external components (RFC 9552), using the same protocol for SR Policies avoids adding another collection protocol. The extensions cover SR-MPLS and SRv6, explicit and dynamic candidate paths, but not composite candidate paths. They complement the BGP SR Policy SAFI (RFC 9830, RFC 9831), which pushes policies from controllers to headends, by reporting operational state back.
sections.eli5: A planner far away can only make good decisions if the routers tell it which special routes they are using. This gives the routers a common way to say so.

sections.title: The SR Policy Candidate Path NLRI
sections.content:
The Link-State NLRI of RFC 9552 is extended with a new NLRI Type, the SR Policy Candidate Path NLRI (value 5), which reports the state of individual candidate paths along with their segment lists. Its fields are a Protocol-ID, an 8-octet Identifier, the Local Node Descriptors TLV (TLV 256) for the headend, and the SR Policy Candidate Path Descriptor TLV. The new Protocol-ID "Segment Routing" (value 9) MUST be used.

The Local Node Descriptors TLV always identifies only the headend of the policy, whoever produces the advertisement. It MUST include at least one of the IPv4 Router-ID (TLV 1028) or IPv6 Router-ID (TLV 1029).

When the headend is the BGP-LS Producer, the descriptors MUST also include the BGP Router-ID (TLV 516) and the Autonomous System (TLV 512). When a PCE is the Producer, it MUST NOT put its own identifiers in the node descriptors. It MAY include the headend's BGP Router-ID, AS number and confederation member if it knows them, and MAY put its own identifiers in the BGP-LS Attribute.
sections.eli5: Each report is like a labeled folder. The label says which router owns the route and which route it is, and the pages inside describe it.

sections.title: The Candidate Path Descriptor
sections.content:
The SR Policy Candidate Path Descriptor TLV (type 554) is mandatory for this NLRI type and identifies a candidate path as defined in RFC 9256. Its length is variable, with valid values of 24, 36 or 48 octets.

It carries a 1-octet Protocol-Origin (which protocol or component instantiated the path), a 1-octet Flags field, and 2 reserved octets. The E flag says the endpoint is an IPv6 address when set and IPv4 when clear. The O flag does the same for the originator address. After that come the Endpoint (4 or 16 octets), the Policy Color (4 octets), the Originator AS Number (4 octets), the Originator Address (4 or 16 octets) and a 4-octet Discriminator. Together these identify one candidate path.
sections.eli5: This is the name tag on the folder: where the route goes, what color it is, who created it, and a number that tells it apart from its siblings.

sections.title: The State TLVs
sections.content:
The details of a candidate path travel in the optional non-transitive BGP-LS Attribute as TLVs and sub-TLVs. Most of them may appear only once per candidate path, and if several are present the first valid one is used and the rest ignored.

  • SR Binding SID (1201) and SRv6 Binding SID (1212): report the binding SID and its status flags, plus the specified BSID if there is one. The SRv6 TLV SHOULD be used for SRv6 BSIDs, since the older SR Binding SID form is deprecated for that purpose.
  • SR Candidate Path State (1202): 8 octets with Priority, Flags and Preference. Flags include administrative shut, active, backup, evaluated, valid SID list, on-demand, delegated, provisioned by controller, drop-upon-invalid, transit policy and currently dropping.
  • SR Policy Name (1213) and SR Candidate Path Name (1203): symbolic names. Their size is RECOMMENDED to be limited to 255 bytes.
  • SR Candidate Path Constraints (1204): flags, a multi-topology ID and an algorithm, plus sub-TLVs for affinity (1208), SRLG (1209), bandwidth (1210), disjoint group (1211), bidirectional group (1214) and metric (1215).
  • SR Segment List (1205): one per SID list, with a weight for load balancing and ordered SR Segment sub-TLVs (1206), plus optional metric (1207), bandwidth (1216) and identifier (1217) sub-TLVs.

Segment sub-TLVs have a Segment Type from 1 to 11, matching the segment types of RFC 9256 (Type A to Type K), each with its own descriptor. Reserved fields MUST be set to 0 by the originator and ignored by a receiver, and undefined flag bits MUST be cleared.
sections.eli5: The inside pages of the folder tell you the route's current mood: is it switched on, is it in use, what rules does it follow, and what exact stops does it make.

sections.title: Procedures
sections.content:
Advertisements for this NLRI type are generally originated by the headend for policies instantiated on its own node. A node such as a PCE may advertise on behalf of the headend. A candidate path may have been instantiated by local configuration, PCEP or BGP SR Policy signaling, and the Protocol-Origin field says which. A PCE producing the advertisement uses the "in PCEP" variants of the Protocol-Origin where available, so its reports can be told apart from headend reports.

The state and attributes are encoded in the BGP-LS Attribute. The Candidate Path State TLV is included to report state, the BSID TLV when a BSID is specified or allocated, the Constraints TLV and its sub-TLVs for constraints and the optimization metric, and one SR Segment List TLV for each SID list. The Segment List Metric sub-TLV reports metric values for a single SID list.

The RFC adds that existing BGP operational and management procedures apply and that no new procedures are defined.
sections.eli5: The router writes up a report for each of its special routes and sends it along. If a helper writes it for the router, the report says so.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions do not affect the base BGP security model, and the security considerations of BGP-LS in RFC 9552 also apply. SR operates within a trusted SR domain (RFC 8402), and the SR Policy information is expected to stay within a single AS or between ASes or domains inside a single provider network. Isolating BGP-LS sessions from sessions for other address families helps ensure the information is not advertised to an external BGP session by accident.

The RFC also notes that exporting this information may risk the confidentiality of commercially sensitive details such as endpoint addresses, SIDs and deployed policies. Because BGP peerings need configuration, the operator is responsible for letting only trusted routers and controller applications receive it.
sections.eli5: The notes are private to the network owner. Only helpers the owner has picked should get a copy.

sections.title: IANA Code Points
sections.content:
IANA allocated NLRI Type 5 (SR Policy Candidate Path NLRI) in the "BGP-LS NLRI Types" registry and Protocol-ID 9 (Segment Routing) in the "BGP-LS Protocol-IDs" registry. It also allocated TLV code points 554 and 1201 to 1217 in the "BGP-LS NLRI and Attribute TLVs" registry.

The RFC also creates registries for the SR Policy Protocol-Origin, the BGP-LS SR Segment Descriptors and the BGP-LS SR Policy Metric Type. Protocol-Origin codes include 1 for PCEP and 2 for BGP SR Policy, with variants 10 and 20 for the "in PCEP" reporting case. Metric types include IGP (0), minimum unidirectional delay (1), TE (2), hop count (3), SID list length (4) and user defined (128 to 255).
sections.eli5: Every new kind of note gets its own official number in a public list, so everybody uses the same numbers.

items.desc: SRLG values excluded from the path.
